Salt selection affects: solubility (determines dissolution rate), stability, hygroscopicity, processing properties, and bioavailability. E.g., metformin HCl vs metformin hydrochloride.

Note: stability, and bioavailability

Additional: drug have different solubility dissolution rate
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is a soft drug?

options.a: A drug that is very easily absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract
options.b: A drug designed to be metabolized to an inactive form
options.c: A drug that dissolves quickly on the tongue without any water
options.d: A drug that produces only very gentle pharmacological effects

explanation:
Soft drugs (e.g., esmolol, loteprednol) are designed to have predictable, rapid metabolism to inactive metabolites after their site of action, reducing systemic side effects.

Additional: after exerting its therapeutic effect limiting duration of action
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is a hard drug?

options.a: A drug that is difficult to administer
options.b: A drug that is not metabolized or minimally metabolized
options.c: A solid drug
options.d: A strong drug

explanation:
Hard drugs resist metabolic degradation (e.g., cyclosporine, diazepam). They remain active for longer but may accumulate and cause more side effects compared to soft drugs.

Additional: maintaining activity throughout its residence in the body
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the significance of the amide bond in peptides and proteins?

options.a: The amide bond has no effect on the shape or stability of proteins
options.b: It provides structural rigidity, stability to hydrolysis
options.c: The amide bond is freely rotating and very easily hydrolyzed in water
options.d: The amide bond is found only in nucleic acids and never in proteins

explanation:
The amide (peptide) bond has partial double bond character due to resonance, making it planar and rigid. This constrains protein folding. It is stable to hydrolysis under physiological conditions.

Note: and serves as the backbone linking amino acids
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the Bischler-Napieralski reaction?

options.a: A condensation reaction between two molecules of a simple ester
options.b: A cyclization of beta-phenylethylamides using P2O5 or POCl3
options.c: An oxidation reaction converting a primary alcohol into an aldehyde
options.d: A reduction reaction converting a nitro group into an amino group

explanation:
Bischler-Napieralski: cyclodehydration of N-acyl-beta-phenylethylamine using Lewis acid (P2O5, POCl3) to form 3,4-dihydroisoquinoline. Key step in synthesizing isoquinoline alkaloids.

Additional: to form dihydroisoquinolines — important in alkaloid synthesis
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the Pictet-Spengler reaction?

options.a: A condensation of two molecules of a simple aliphatic ketone
options.b: A condensation of a beta-arylethylamine with an aldehyde
options.c: A dehydration reaction that forms an alkene from a primary alcohol
options.d: A nucleophilic substitution reaction on an aromatic ring by an amine

explanation:
Pictet-Spengler: beta-arylethylamine + aldehyde → Schiff base → acid-catalyzed ring closure → tetrahydroisoquinoline. Important in biosynthesis and synthesis of alkaloids.

Additional: aldehyde/ketone followed by cyclization to form tetrahydroisoquinolines
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the Curtius rearrangement?

options.a: A rearrangement of alkenes to cyclopropanes
options.b: Thermal decomposition of an acyl azide to an isocyanate with loss of nitrogen
options.c: A condensation reaction of two aldehydes
options.d: A reduction reaction of a nitro group

explanation:
Curtius: RCON3 → R-N=C=O + N2. The isocyanate is hydrolyzed to amine. Used to convert carboxylic acids to amines with one fewer carbon atom.

Additional: loss of N2 used to convert carboxylic acids to amines
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the Hofmann rearrangement?

options.a: A reaction in which primary alcohols are dehydrated to alkenes
options.b: Conversion of a primary amide to a primary amine with one fewer carbon atom, using bromine and alkali
options.c: An oxidation of primary amines to nitro compounds using strong oxidants
options.d: A condensation of two amide molecules with elimination of ammonia

explanation:
Hofmann: RCONH2 + Br2 + 4NaOH → RNH2 + Na2CO3 + 2NaBr. Converts primary amide to amine with loss of carbonyl carbon (one fewer carbon).

Additional: amine with one fewer carbon using Br2/NaOH
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the Gabriel phthalimide synthesis?

options.a: A method to synthesize carboxylic acids
options.b: A method to prepare pure primary amines from alkyl halides
options.c: A method to synthesize esters
options.d: A method to prepare alcohols

explanation:
Gabriel synthesis: phthalimide + KOH → potassium phthalimide, then + R-X → N-alkylphthalimide, then hydrazinolysis → pure primary amine (RNH2). Avoids over-alkylation problem.

Additional: alkyl halides via phthalimide intermediate avoiding polyalkylation
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the significance of the phenol group in drug molecules?

options.a: It has no significance
options.b: Phenols can form hydrogen bonds
options.c: Phenols are always toxic
options.d: Phenols cannot participate in reactions

explanation:
Phenols are important: hydrogen bond donors/acceptors, can be oxidized, electron-rich aromatic ring participates in EAS, common pharmacophore in analgesics (salicylates), hormones (estradiol), and neurotransmitters.

Note: and are common in many drugs; salicylates, morphine, tyrosine

Note: undergo oxidation to quinones
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the significance of the carboxylic acid group in drugs?

options.a: It serves only to make the drug acidic and has no other useful function
options.b: It enables salt formation for solubility, participates in hydrogen bonding
options.c: It is always removed from the molecule during first-pass metabolism
options.d: It prevents the drug from binding to plasma proteins in the blood

explanation:
Carboxylic acids: enable salt formation (improving solubility), act as hydrogen bond donors/acceptors, can be esterified for prodrugs, and are present in NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen, diclofenac).

Note: and can be modified to esters (prodrugs) or amides
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the significance of the amino group in drug molecules?

options.a: It has no significance
options.b: Amino groups can be protonated
options.c: Amino groups make drugs inactive
options.d: Amino groups are toxic always

explanation:
Amino groups: protonate at physiological pH (forming water-soluble salts), hydrogen bond, participate in nucleophilic reactions, found in many drugs (sulfonamides, local anesthetics, antihistamines).

Note: and are common in many drugs

Note: forming salts for solubility

Note: participate in hydrogen bonding
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the significance of the halogen atom in drug design?

options.a: Bromine substitution always reduces the lipophilicity of an aromatic drug
options.b: Fluorine enhances metabolic stability and lipophilicity, improving drug action
options.c: Iodine substitution has no effect at all on the metabolic half-life of a drug
options.d: Adding a halogen to a molecule always increases its water solubility

explanation:
Halogens in drug design: F (increases metabolic stability, bioisostere for H, improves membrane permeability), Cl/Br (increase lipophilicity, can form halogen bonds with proteins), I (used in radiocontrast).

Additional: increase lipophilicity and can participate in binding

Note: chlorine/bromine
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the difference between a drug's intrinsic activity and efficacy?

options.a: Intrinsic activity is the dose of a drug that produces half of the maximum response
options.b: Intrinsic activity is the ability to activate a receptor; efficacy is the resulting response
options.c: Efficacy refers to the affinity of the drug for its binding site on the receptor
options.d: Intrinsic activity describes the rate at which a drug is absorbed and distributed

explanation:
Intrinsic activity (a): ability of drug to activate receptor (full agonist a=1, partial agonist 0<a<1, antagonist a=0). Efficacy: maximum therapeutic effect achievable in a clinical setting.

Note: 0-1 scale

Additional: is the maximum response a drug can produce in vivo

Note: efficacy
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the Clark's occupancy theory?

options.a: A theory describing how much space a drug occupies in the body after injection
options.b: A theory stating that drug response is proportional to receptor occupancy
options.c: A theory about how drugs should be stored to occupy less warehouse space
options.d: A theory of how cells rearrange themselves to occupy tissue in an organ

explanation:
Clark's theory: Drug response = proportion of receptors occupied. Occupancy depends on drug concentration and receptor affinity (Kd). Limitations: doesn't account for spare receptors or partial agonists.

Additional: the fraction of receptors occupied by the drug
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the difference between affinity and potency?

options.a: Affinity is the clinical effect produced while potency is the strength of receptor binding
options.b: Affinity is how well a drug binds to a receptor; potency is the dose needed for effect
options.c: Potency measures how tightly the drug binds to the receptor at its site
options.d: Affinity measures the size of the clinical effect the drug can produce

explanation:
Affinity (Kd): binding strength to receptor (measured in binding assays). Potency (EC50): concentration needed for 50% of maximum effect (functional assays). A high-affinity drug may have low potency if it has low intrinsic activity.

Additional: is the amount of drug needed to produce a given effect
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the chemical structure of penicillin G (benzylpenicillin)?

options.a: 6-APA with a benzyl side chain
options.b: Penicillin nucleus with a phenylacetamido
options.c: A cephalosporin structure
options.d: A macrolide structure

explanation:
Penicillin G: 6-phenylacetamidopenicillanic acid. It has the beta-lactam ring fused to thiazolidine ring, with a phenylacetamido group at C-6. Active against Gram-positive bacteria.

Note: beta-lactam + thiazolidine

Additional: side chain at position 6
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: Why is penicillin G acid-labile (destroyed in stomach acid)?

options.a: The thiazolidine ring becomes saturated and loses its sulfur atom in acid
options.b: The beta-lactam ring is susceptible to acid-catalyzed hydrolysis
options.c: The carboxyl group undergoes rapid decarboxylation in the acidic stomach
options.d: The molecule is destroyed by the high ionic strength of the gastric juice

explanation:
The beta-lactam ring is strained and susceptible to acid-catalyzed hydrolysis. Protonation of the carbonyl oxygen activates the ring toward nucleophilic attack by water, opening the lactam.

Additional: opened by protonation of the amide carbonyl
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: How were acid-stable penicillins developed?

options.a: By changing the thiazolidine ring
options.b: By introducing an electron-withdrawing group
options.c: By removing the beta-lactam ring
options.d: By adding more benzyl groups

explanation:
Penicillin V (phenoxymethylpenicillin) has an electron-withdrawing oxygen next to the amide nitrogen, which reduces the nucleophilicity of the amide nitrogen and decreases acid-catalyzed beta-lactam ring opening.

Note: reducing beta-lactam ring opening

Note: e.g., phenoxymethyl in penicillin V

Additional: adjacent to the amide nitrogen
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the role of the acyl side chain in penicillin activity?

options.a: It has no role
options.b: The side chain determines spectrum
options.c: It only affects solubility
options.d: It makes penicillin inactive

explanation:
The acyl side chain at C-6 determines: antibacterial spectrum (Gram-positive vs broad-spectrum), acid stability, beta-lactamase susceptibility, and protein binding.

Note: and resistance to beta-lactamase

Additional: of activity acid stability
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the Vilsmeier-Haack reaction?

options.a: A hydrolysis reaction in which an ester is cleaved by dilute acid
options.b: A formylation reaction using DMF and POCl3 to introduce a formyl group
options.c: An oxidation reaction converting a primary alcohol into an aldehyde
options.d: A reduction reaction that converts a nitro group into an amino group

explanation:
Vilsmeier-Haack: DMF + POCl3 generates a chloroiminium ion that acts as an electrophile, introducing a formyl group (-CHO) on electron-rich aromatics and heterocycles.

Additional: introduce a -CHO group on electron-rich aromatic rings
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the Sandmeyer reaction?

options.a: Reaction of an aromatic compound with concentrated sulfuric acid
options.b: Replacement of a diazonium group with -Cl, -Br
options.c: A reduction reaction applied to aromatic nitro compounds
options.d: A hydrolysis reaction in which an ester is cleaved by water

explanation:
Sandmeyer: Ar-N2+ + CuX → Ar-X (X = Cl, Br, CN). Aromatic diazonium salts are converted to aryl halides or nitriles using copper(I) chloride/bromide/cyanide.

Note: or -CN using copper(I) salts as catalysts
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the Fries rearrangement?

options.a: A thermal rearrangement of alkyl groups between two aromatic rings
options.b: Lewis acid-catalyzed rearrangement of phenyl esters
options.c: A condensation reaction between two molecules of a phenol
options.d: A reduction reaction converting a ketone into a secondary alcohol

explanation:
Fries rearrangement: phenyl ester + AlCl3 → ortho- and para-acylphenols. Position of product depends on temperature (low temp favors para; high temp favors ortho).

Additional: to give ortho- and para-hydroxyaryl ketones
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the significance of the oxazolidinone ring?

options.a: No significance
options.b: It is the pharmacophore of oxazolidinone
options.c: It is found in all antibiotics
options.d: It is a metabolite only

explanation:
The oxazolidinone ring (with a carbonyl at C-2 and substituents at C-5) is essential for the antibacterial activity of linezolid and tedizolid, which inhibit the 50S ribosomal subunit.

Additional: antibiotics that inhibits bacterial protein synthesis

question_text: What is the significance of the 3-OH group in morphine?

options.c: It is the only group that allows morphine to form salts with acids
options.d: It must remain free for morphine to cross the blood-brain barrier
